scenario: AITA for “cheating” my family out of hundreds of dollars? | I have a giant family. My mom and my dad both have a lot of siblings and they’re also both the youngest in their families. This means I’m nearly the youngest of over 20 cousins. We all live close so we throw gigantic family get togethers. All the time. My grandparents own a pretty big ranch just outside of town. They’re not rich by any means, but land is cheap out here and they’ve owned the property for a long time. Because these gatherings sometimes attract upwards of 40 people, their ranch has been the venue of choice for as long as I can remember. My uncles are all stereotypically masculine dudes, as are a lot of my older cousins, so our rendezvous generally revolve around sports, grilling, and gambling. Gambling isn’t exactly my cup of tea, but I participate for the sake of being social. I usually lose a fair bit of money because I don’t play cards or know sports teams as well as everybody else. It’s gotten to the point where it’s become a reoccurring joke amongst family members. Well this time around we have an especially large gathering. So large that It’s determined there’s too many people to coordinate our typical gambling games. To make things simpler, my aunt comes up with an idea. She fills a jar full of beans and places it high up on the mantle. She tells us it’s $20 a guess and whoever guesses closest to the number of beans inside gets to take home all the money. For whatever reason this new form of betting got everyone in an especially adversarial spirit. Almost all of the adults participated and many even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Remember how I’m typically ignorant when it comes to gambling? Well this time I was in my element. I could tell the jar was a typical 64oz mason jar, which a quick Google search told me was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Divide the jar by the beans and I got 773. Then I assumed 20% of it was air, which left me with ~619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and the other for 630. As I’m making my bet, people are giving me crap like “it’d be easier if you just gave it directly to me” and all the other usual ball busting, but I just smile and say nothing. Some can tell something’s up and continue to give me grief for the rest of the night. After probably 40 minutes of interrupted counting, my aunt informed everyone that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anybody else’s. At first everybody was super happy for me, laughing about how lucky I am. One of the suspicious cousins from earlier asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately I could see people’s faces start to sour. One of my uncles said “that’s bullshit” and left the room. It ended up being nearly $1100. My parents tell me that I should offer to return it because I didn’t earn it fairly. I argue that I had all the same information as everybody else. AITA for keeping the money?

message.reasoning: Okay, so I'm trying to figure out whether I did something wrong by keeping the $1100 I won at the family gathering. Let me start by understanding the situation better. First, the family gatherings are a big deal. We have a lot of cousins, and we all live close, so getting together is common. My grandparents have a ranch where we usually meet, and these gatherings often involve sports, grilling, and gambling. I'm not really into gambling, but I participate to be social. Usually, I lose money because I don't know much about cards or sports teams. It's become a running joke among family members. This time, the gathering was especially large, so my aunt came up with a new idea to make things simpler. She filled a jar with beans and placed it on the mantel. She said it was $20 a guess, and whoever guessed closest to the number of beans would take home all the money. Almost everyone participated, and some even made multiple guesses to increase their odds. Now, I'm usually not good at gambling, but this time I felt like I was in my element. I knew the jar was a typical 64 oz Mason jar, which I quickly looked up and found out was 116 cubic inches in volume. I also found that a bean was about 0.15 cubic inches. Dividing the jar's volume by the bean's volume gave me approximately 773 beans. I assumed 20% of the jar was air, which left me with about 619 beans. To be safe, I made two bets: one for 610 and another for 630. When I was making my bets, people were teasing me, saying things like, "It'd be easier if you just gave it directly to me," but I just smiled and didn't say anything. Some people could tell I was onto something and continued to tease me throughout the night. After about 40 minutes of counting, my aunt announced that not only had I won, but both of my guesses were closer than anyone else's. At first, everyone was happy for me, laughing about how lucky I was. One of the suspicious cousins asked how I did it, so I told everyone my strategy. Immediately, I could see people's faces start to sour. One of my uncles said, "That's bullsh*t," and left the room. In the end, I won nearly $1100. My parents told me I should offer to return it because I didn't earn it fairly. I argued that I had all the same information as everyone else. Now, I'm wondering if I did something wrong by keeping the money. So, is it right or wrong for me to keep the money? Let's break this down. First, I used my knowledge of math and volume to estimate the number of beans in the jar. I made two guesses to increase my chances. I didn't cheat; I just used my skills to make an educated guess. I told everyone my strategy when they asked, so there was no deception involved. However, some family members were upset because they felt I had an unfair advantage. They might have thought that since I'm not usually good at gambling, I shouldn't have been able to win so much. My uncle even accused me of lying and left the room. My parents think I should return the money because they believe I didn't earn it fairly. But I feel like I did earn it because I used my skills and knowledge, just like anyone else could have if they knew how to calculate it. Is there a clear right or wrong here? It seems like a gray area. On one hand, I didn't cheat; I just used my abilities. On the other hand, some family members felt I had an unfair advantage, which might have made them uncomfortable or upset. Maybe the issue is more about how the game was set up. If the game relies on guessing the number of beans, and some people have better estimation skills, then it's inherently not a completely fair game. But in this case, I used math to estimate, which is a legitimate strategy. I also told everyone my strategy when they asked, so there was transparency. If they were upset, maybe it's because they felt I had an unfair advantage, but I didn't hide anything. In the end, I think it's a matter of perspective. If I feel like I earned the money fairly, even if others are upset, then maybe it's not wrong to keep it. However, if keeping the money causes tension or hurt feelings within the family, it might be better to return it to maintain harmony. I also need to consider the impact on family relationships. If keeping the money leads to arguments or resentment, it might not be worth it, even if I technically didn't do anything wrong. Family harmony is important, and sometimes compromising is necessary. So, in conclusion, while I didn't cheat, the situation has caused discomfort among some family members. It might be better to return the money to avoid further conflict, even if I believe I earned it fairly.
